comparison: Both strongly support the core finding that trypanosomatid PKA is activated by nucleosides rather than cyclic nucleotides (C2, C34-C49, C61-C66). OpenEval emphasizes the comprehensive experimental evidence including kinase assays, ITC measurements, and SAR analysis. Peer reviewers describe the work as providing 'exceptional evidence' and being 'thorough and convincing.' Both evaluations are fully aligned in supporting these claims.

Both support the SAR data (C35, C40-C45) establishing structural requirements for nucleoside binding. OpenEval includes these claims within the broader experimental validation, while peer reviewers accept them as part of the 'extensive experimental work' without specific critique. Full agreement on these detailed structure-activity relationships.

Both strongly support the mutagenesis and structural findings (C3, C68-C92) demonstrating conversion of specificity. OpenEval highlights the high-resolution crystal structures and systematic residue analysis. Peer Reviewer 3 specifically notes the identification of 2-3 residues controlling specificity as 'of particular interest.' Complete concordance on the mutagenesis and structural evidence.

Both support the crystal structure data (C68-C72, C83-C86) showing nucleoside binding determinants. OpenEval emphasizes the high resolution (1.4-2.1 Å) and validation through mutant 6 structure with cAMP. Peer Reviewer 3 explicitly accepts the structural dissection of binding determinants. Full agreement on structural findings.

Both support the αD helix findings (C4-C5, C93-C100, C123) including structural positioning, conservation, and functional validation through mutant 8. OpenEval provides detailed analysis of the structural data and 82-fold affinity decrease. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings as part of the 'exceptional evidence' and 'thorough' investigation. Complete agreement.

Both support the site-selective binding and synergistic activation findings (C6, C101-C109). OpenEval notes the sound experimental design using site-specific mutants and acknowledges the limitation of measuring binding to 'primed' protein. Peer Reviewer 3 accepts the dissection of binding determinants. Full concordance with OpenEval providing more methodological detail.

Both support the in vivo ligand identification (C7-C8, C115-C118) through mass spectrometry. OpenEval emphasizes the quantitative rigor from stable isotope standards and comprehensive database search, while noting potential limitations. Peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the comprehensive experimental approach without challenge. Full agreement.

Both support the mechanistic interpretation (C110-C114) that both binding sites are required for efficient activation based on EC50/KD ratios. OpenEval notes consistency with mammalian PKA mechanisms while suggesting structural evidence would strengthen conclusions. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this mechanistic model through their overall positive assessment. Complete concordance.

Both support the evolutionary and structural conservation findings (C119-C121). OpenEval notes the claims are somewhat speculative about evolutionary precedence without direct holoenzyme evidence. Peer Reviewer 1 accepts the work as 'a significant advancement in understanding cyclic nucleotide binding domains,' implicitly supporting the evolutionary interpretations. Agreement with OpenEval noting greater caution.

Both support the methodological findings (C53-C60) regarding E. coli-derived ligand binding and refolding protocols. OpenEval provides detailed analysis of the boiling/activation experiments and nanoDSF validation, noting the stoichiometry issue. Peer reviewers accept these as part of the 'thorough' experimental approach without specific comment. Full agreement.

Significant disagreement on speculative claims (C122, C124). OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN, noting they are speculative interpretations lacking direct evidence for other CNB ligands or energetic measurements. Peer reviewers do not challenge these claims and Reviewer 1 accepts the broader implications about CNB domain versatility. Peer reviewers are more accepting of speculative interpretations than OpenEval.

OpenEval supports the thermodynamic comparison (C67) showing similar binding mechanisms despite different ligands. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific minor observation, though it would likely be accepted as part of the comprehensive experimental work.

OpenEval categorizes background/context claims (C1, C9-C33) as supported by literature citations. These are not specifically evaluated by peer reviewers as they represent established knowledge rather than novel findings. No disagreement, but peer review focuses on novel contributions.
